newsitem.title: UK: Britain's parties unveil election manifestos.
newsitem.headline: Britain's parties unveil election manifestos.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major offered 25 "pledges for the nation" in his party's manifesto.

Labour leader Tony Blair countered on Thursday with a 10-point "contract with the people" ahead of the May 1 election and on Friday Liberal Democrat Paddy Ashdown accused both of offering puny solutions and offered his own recipe.
Here are the key promises in the three manifestos:
TAX AND SPENDING

- The Conservatives promise tight control of spending, aiming for a 20 percent basic rate of income tax. They promise low inflation policies. Major offered tax breaks for families where one partner is looking after children or relatives.

- Labour pledges no increases in the basic or top rates of tax, with an "objective" of a 10 percent starting rate. It will also set "tough" targets for inflation and keep within the government's published spending levels.

- The Liberal Democrats would raise the basic rate of income tax by a penny to fund education improvements and raise tax allowances by setting a new 50 percent tax rate on incomes over 100,000 stg a year. They want an independent Bank of England.
EDUCATION

- Major's manifesto promises more independence for schools, creating a "grammar school" -- schools geared towards academic performance -- in every town. It also promises more rigorous appraisal of teachers and targets for school performance.

- Blair's "number one priority". Labour would boost nursery education, cut class sizes in primary schools, set minimum standards for homework and improve teacher training, while closing down failing schools.

- The extra 2 billion a year Ashdown plans to raise would provide pre-school places for all toddlers, increase funding for books and equipment, reduce primary school class sizes and tackle repair backlogs.
JOBS
- Major says staying out of the European Union's Social Chapter will protect jobs and promises to continue a scheme requiring the long-term unemployed to go on work experience.

- Blair promises to get 250,000 young unemployed off benefit and into work through a jobs scheme funded by a "windfall tax" on privatised utilities -- the only spending commitment of a manifesto geared to bury the party's old "tax and spend" image.
- Liberal Democrats would allow the long-term unemployed to turn their dole into "working benefits" paid to employers to recruit and train them.
HEALTH
- Major promises to increase the real resources given to the National Health Service and bring in private-sector investment.
- Labour is pledging to cut the money spent on administration, channelling it instead to patient care.
- The Liberals plan free eye and dental checks and more NHS staff, paid for partly by more tax on cigarettes.
LAW AND ORDER

- The Conservatives, traditionally the party of law and order, promises a crackdown on petty crime, more closed circuit television cameras in towns and automatic life sentences for anyone convicted of a second serious sexual or violent crime.
- Labour, in Blair's words, promises to be "tough on crime and tough on the causes of crime" as well as halving the time it takes to take persistent juvenile offenders to court.
- The Liberals pledge to put an extra 3,000 police on the beat within a year of the election.
WELFARE

- The Conservatives promise a crackdown on welfare cheats and reform to the pension system, with all young people coming into the workforce paying into a personal pension fund. Changes will ensure old people can insure against future care costs.

- Labour would retain the state old-age pension, while creating second pensions for those on low and modest incomes and setting up a Royal Commission to work out a fair system for funding long-term care for the elderly.
- The Liberals would seek cross-party consensus on a review of the welfare system aimed at providing a more effective safety net, encouraging work and widening opportunities.
POLITICS
- Major, warning that Labour's plans would lead to the break-up of the United Kingdom, promises an "evolutionary -- rather than revolutionary -- approach to constitutional change.

- Blair, capitalising on sleaze allegations that have dogged the Conservatives, wants to clean up politics and donations, reform the House of Lords and devolve power to Scotland and Wales through referendums offering seperate assemblies.
- Ashdown backs Blair's reform agenda, but unlike the Labour leader, promises to campaign for change in a referendum on whether to replace the first-past-the post voting system.
EUROPE AND FOREIGN POLICY

- In perhaps the most distinct policy of the whole manifesto, Major pledged not to allow Britain to become part of a federal European state, maintaining the country's veto and border controls, and keeping the options open on whether or not to join a single currency.

- Although promising a referendum before entering a single currency, Blair promises a centre role in Europe, signing the Social Chapter and forging alliances with other states to enlarge the European Union and reform the Common Agricultural Policy, while retaining a veto over areas like border controls.

- Ashdown says it is in Britain's interests to join a single currency provided it and its partners meet the Maastricht criteria and a referendum endorses the move. But he is not starry-eyed over Europe -- he says the fisheries policy should be scrapped and the farm policy much reformed. -- London Newsroom +44 171 5427767
